## Requirement

docs/plan.md, "Tools": "Native Go tools first: `bash` (policy-gated), `read`/`write`/`edit`, `fetch`, **`search`**." The plan names `search` as a member of the native tool set alongside the file tools — i.e. filesystem/content search, distinct from `recall` (which searches conversation memory via FTS5, `internal/memory`).

## Current behaviour

`internal/tool/builtin.go` registers exactly five builtins: `bash` (:43), `read_file` (:97), `write_file` (:131), `edit_file` (:173), `fetch` (:226). There is no `search`. The registry (`Builtins`, `internal/tool/toolbox.go`) is what both the host toolbox and the sandbox runner (`internal/sandbox/toolbox.go`) draw from, so the gap is uniform across execution modes.

Today the model compensates with `bash` + `grep`/`find`/`rg`. That works only when three things line up:

1. **Policy allows `bash`.** The whole point of a tool allow/deny list (`tool.Restrict`, and per-group policy once #33 lands) is that risky contexts get file tools *without* shell. In such a session the model can read any file it can name but cannot *find* files — a crippled read tier.
2. **The binaries exist.** The default sandbox image is `debian:stable-slim` (`internal/sandbox/docker.go:59`); minimal images may lack `rg` and even `find` variants the model assumes. The model burns iterations discovering this.
3. **The model writes portable flags.** `grep -r --include` vs BSD/GNU differences etc. — a native tool removes a whole class of flailing.

## Impact

Functional completeness plus a real policy consequence: **"no shell, read-only file access" is not a usable tier without search**, and that tier is exactly what #33 (trust tiering) and #66 (action-level policy) want to hand to risky contexts. Cost is also non-trivial: shell-based search failures consume agent iterations (bounded at 50, `internal/agent/agent.go:73`) and tokens.

## Proposed change

A `search` builtin in `internal/tool/builtin.go`, pure Go, no subprocess:

- **Input:** `{ "pattern": <Go regexp>, "path": <root dir>, "glob": <optional filename filter>, "max_results": <optional> }`.
- **Behaviour:** `filepath.WalkDir` from `path`; skip `.git` and other VCS dirs; apply `glob` to basenames; regexp-match file contents line by line; return `path:line: excerpt` rows.
- **Bounding, consistent with the existing tools:** cap matched lines per file and total results (documented defaults, e.g. 5/100); cap per-line excerpt length; run the aggregate output through `Truncate(…, OutputLimit)` like `read_file`/`fetch` (`builtin.go:263`); skip binary files (NUL-byte sniff on the first block); enforce a per-call file-size ceiling and an overall walk deadline from `ctx`.
- **Registration:** same builtin set, so host toolbox, sandbox runner, and MCP-facing definitions all get it with no extra wiring; tool description states results are data, mirroring `fetch`'s untrusted-content note where appropriate.

### Alternative (explicitly on the table)

If `bash`-as-search is the deliberate design, the correct resolution is instead a docs/plan.md amendment removing `search` from the native list and stating the rationale — that path belongs to #39 (plan-drift sweep). One or the other must happen; the plan and the binary currently disagree.

### Non-goals

- No indexing/caching layer; every call walks fresh (personal-scale trees).
- No fuzzy or semantic search (that's #60's territory, over memory, not files).
- No replacement of `recall` — different corpus, both stay.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `search` appears in `Builtins` with schema, description, and result caps documented in the tool description (the model reads it).
- [ ] Matches return as `path:line: excerpt` with per-file and total caps enforced; a run over a tree with more matches than the cap says so explicitly in the output tail (mirroring `Truncate`'s marker convention).
- [ ] Binary files are skipped; a test includes a file with NUL bytes and asserts it produces no matches and no error.
- [ ] `.git` directories are not walked (test).
- [ ] Invalid regexp returns a tool error naming the pattern, not a panic (test).
- [ ] Context cancellation mid-walk aborts promptly (test with a short deadline over a large synthetic tree).
- [ ] The sandbox runner exposes `search` with identical behaviour (covered by the existing sandbox toolbox pass-through tests, extended if needed).
- [ ] A policy-restricted toolbox of `{read_file, search}` (no bash) can complete a "find where X is defined" exercise in an agent-loop test — the tier is demonstrably usable.
- [ ] docs/plan.md's tool list matches reality after this lands (either the tool exists, or the plan is amended — checkbox satisfied by whichever resolution is chosen, recorded in #39's sweep).

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#33 (trust tiering) / #66 (action-level policy):** this tool is what makes their restricted read-only tier practical.
- **#39 (plan drift):** shares the "plan vs. reality" reconciliation; if the alternative resolution is chosen, it merges into #39's sweep.
- **#69 (truncation at capture):** output bounding here should follow whatever spill-file convention #69 establishes, if that lands first.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Native `search` tool from the plan's tool set is missing: read-only sessions fall back to shell for the most common read operation

## Requirement

docs/plan.md, "Self-development loop" step 4: doctor's self-check is "config parses, DB migrates on a copy, secret store round-trips, **providers reachable**." The upgrade gate relies on doctor (`internal/selfdev/selfdev.go` runs the *new* binary's `doctor` before swapping), so a "providers reachable" check is not just a health nicety — it's part of what makes `waffle upgrade` safe.

## Current behaviour

`Doctor` (`internal/selfdev/selfdev.go:35-95`) implements the first three checks and then **discards the loaded config**:

- `add("config parses", …)` — `selfdev.go:50`
- `add("database snapshot", …)` / `add("database migrates", …)` — `selfdev.go:66,73`
- `add("secret store opens", …)` / `add("secret store", …, "skipped")` — `selfdev.go:83,85`
- `_ = cfg` — `selfdev.go:88` — the loaded config, including the entire provider section, is thrown away. The provider is **never probed**.

So the fourth check the plan names simply doesn't exist.

## Impact

`waffle upgrade` can swap in a binary whose provider setup is broken — bad `base_url`, missing or undecryptable API key, unreachable endpoint — and doctor reports **all green**, so the gate passes and the swap happens. The failure then surfaces only on the next real conversation (a cron job at 3am, or the owner's next message), as a runtime provider error, with the healthy-looking upgrade already in place. It also weakens `waffle doctor` as a standalone "is my box healthy?" command — the one check that exercises the credit-card-spending path is absent.

## Proposed change

Add a "provider reachable" check using the already-loaded `cfg` (the `_ = cfg` line is the seam):

1. For each configured provider, resolve its API-key ref through the secret store, then make a **minimal authenticated request** with a short timeout — the cheapest call the provider offers (a 1-token completion, or a models-list/ping endpoint). Success = reachable + authenticated.
2. **Degrade gracefully**, matching the existing secret-store check's pattern: if no key is configured for a provider, report `skipped` (like `secret store … "no identity configured (skipped)"`, `selfdev.go:85`) rather than failing — an unconfigured provider isn't a broken one.
3. A genuine failure (auth rejected, endpoint unreachable, key undecryptable) reports **red**, which fails the upgrade gate — exactly the outcome the plan wants.
4. Keep the timeout short and the network call optional-by-design so `doctor` stays fast and works offline (offline → the reachability check reports its network failure honestly; it shouldn't hang).

The check plumbing already exists — `add(name, err, info)` (`selfdev.go`) is the exact shape to reuse.

### Non-goals

- Not a full provider capability probe (model availability, feature detection) — just "authenticated request succeeds."
- Not retrying/backoff — one short-timeout attempt; doctor reports what it saw.
- Not changing the other three checks.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Doctor` performs a provider-reachability check per configured provider using the loaded `cfg`; the `_ = cfg` discard is gone.
- [ ] With a reachable provider and a valid key, the check reports pass; a test uses a stub/`httptest` provider endpoint (no live API calls).
- [ ] With no key configured, the check reports `skipped`, not fail (test).
- [ ] With an unreachable endpoint or rejected auth, the check reports fail, and a test asserts that a failing provider check causes the aggregate `ok` to be false (so the upgrade gate would block the swap).
- [ ] The check honors a short timeout and does not hang when the endpoint is unreachable (test with a non-routable/blocked address or a stub that never responds + deadline).
- [ ] Undecryptable/missing key ref is reported as a clear failure/skip (not a panic) — test.
- [ ] `waffle doctor` output lists the provider check alongside the existing ones.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#42 (docker runner probe):** another doctor check the plan implies; both extend the same `add(...)` machinery — land them consistently.
- **#39 (plan drift):** this closes one of the plan-vs-reality deltas; check it off in #39's sweep.
- **#43 (spend limits):** the reachability probe spends a trivial amount; note it should be exempt from / trivially within any configured budget so doctor never trips its own limit.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: waffle doctor never checks provider reachability: the loaded config is discarded, so upgrade can swap in a binary with broken provider setup and still gate green

## Requirement

docs/plan.md, "Repo workspaces" lifecycle:

- Step 3 (Idle): "**After a configurable idle timeout the container *stops*** but the volume persists."
- Step 4 (Close): "On explicit close **or TTL expiry**, waffle verifies the branch is pushed…"

Both the automatic idle-stop and the TTL-close are stated lifecycle behaviors. Neither exists; only the manual CLI verbs do.

## Current behaviour

- `internal/workspace/workspace.go:353-367` — `Manager.Idle` exists and works, but is only invoked from the CLI (`cmd/waffle/ws_cmd.go:64-72`) and from `Close`'s error-restore paths. There is no timer, no last-activity tracking, and no idle/TTL knob in `internal/config/config.go`.
- `Manager.Resume` (`workspace.go:369`) already re-starts an idled container on demand, so "stop when idle, resume when needed" is half-built — the resume half.
- Nothing records per-workspace last activity; the sandbox client timestamps queue traffic, but that isn't persisted to the workspace row.

So every `waffle ws open` leaves a container running until the operator remembers `ws idle`/`ws close`. On an always-on personal box, forgotten workspaces pile up as running containers consuming memory/CPU — exactly what the idle tier was designed to prevent — and TTL-close never fires, so volumes for abandoned work linger.

## Impact

Resource leak by default. The plan's efficiency story ("stop idle containers, keep the cheap volume, resume tomorrow") is unrealized, so the operator pays the running-container cost for every workspace they ever opened until manual cleanup. Not a security issue, but a real operational one on the target deployment. Composes badly with #51 (issue-driven intake multiplies workspace churn) and #46 (each un-reaped container is unbounded per #46, and there are more of them here).

## Proposed change

1. **Track last activity** per workspace: add a `last_active` column (new migration) updated on each `Exec`/queue round trip, or persist the sandbox client's existing timestamp to the workspace row. This is the signal both timers key off.
2. **Auto-idle** under `waffle serve` (a lightweight ticker in the ws manager, or a scheduler-driven sweep): stop containers whose `last_active` is older than `idle_timeout`, mark them idle. Resume-on-demand already handles pickup.
3. **Auto-close on TTL** (longer horizon): past `close_ttl`, run `Manager.Close` **with the existing unpushed-work guard — never `--force`**. A workspace with unpushed work past TTL is *reported/notified*, not destroyed (deliver through the owner's channel, machinery exists in `internal/schedule`).
4. **Config:** `[workspace] idle_timeout = "30m"`, `close_ttl = "168h"`, `0` disables either. Documented defaults.

### Non-goals

- Not `--force` auto-close ever — unpushed work is sacred; TTL past dirty state notifies, doesn't delete.
- Not per-repo TTL overrides in v1 (composes later with #53).
- Not a cross-process reaper design beyond "runs under serve" — but see #48: the sweep must be single-owner (only the `serve` process reaps) to avoid two processes racing on the same container.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `last_active` (or equivalent) timestamp is persisted per workspace and updated on activity; migration is idempotent and passes doctor's migrate check.
- [ ] Under `serve`, a workspace idle longer than `idle_timeout` is stopped and marked idle; a test drives the sweep with a stubbed clock and asserts `Idle` is called for the stale workspace and **not** for a recently-active one.
- [ ] A subsequent request to an auto-idled workspace resumes it (existing `Resume` path) — regression test.
- [ ] Past `close_ttl`, a **clean** workspace is closed via `Manager.Close` (no force); a **dirty** workspace is not closed and instead produces an owner notification — both tested with a stub deliverer and the unpushed-work guard exercised.
- [ ] `[workspace] idle_timeout`/`close_ttl` parse, accept duration strings, and `0` disables the respective timer (tested); defaults documented.
- [ ] The sweep is a no-op when no `serve` is running (CLI-only invocations don't spuriously reap) and is single-owner to avoid the #48 race.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#48 (ws races serve):** the reaper must run only in the `serve` process and coordinate with the instance-lock story there, or two processes fight over containers.
- **#46 (resource limits):** bounds each container; this bounds how many run. Complementary.
- **#51 (issue-driven intake) / #54 (lifecycle hooks):** both multiply/raise workspace churn and want a `before_remove` hook to run before auto-close — coordinate the close path with #54.
- **#55 (observability):** auto-idle/close events belong in the status snapshot.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Workspaces never auto-idle or expire: the plan's "configurable idle timeout" and close-on-TTL are manual-only, so forgotten containers accumulate indefinitely

## Requirement

Two connected promises in docs/plan.md:

- "Repo workspaces": "**Network egress is policy-controlled per workspace (none / allowlist via host egress proxy / full).**"
- "Secret management", broker face 3: "*HTTP:* an **egress proxy** that injects `Authorization` headers for allowlisted hosts, so a sandboxed tool can call an API it is entitled to without ever seeing the key."

These are the same mechanism seen from two sides: a per-workspace policy that decides *whether/where* a container may reach the network, and a broker face that *is* the allowlist path — and, crucially, lets a sandboxed tool use a credentialed API **without holding the credential**.

## Current behaviour

- `internal/workspace/workspace.go:66-68,92` — `Network` defaults to `"bridge"` (full egress) with no config knob and no per-workspace policy; `internal/workspace/runtime.go:65` passes it straight to `docker run --network`. Every workspace therefore gets unrestricted outbound.
- `internal/broker/broker.go` — the broker serves the provider proxy and `/git-credential` only. The package's own comment still advertises an egress face that never shipped ("the git and egress faces arrive with …"); the git face landed, egress did not. A repo-wide grep for "egress" outside docs matches only comments.
- So the plan's `none` and `allowlist` tiers do not exist, and there is no way for a sandboxed tool to call an entitled API without being handed its key — the exact anti-pattern the broker was built to prevent.

## Impact

Given the plan's threat model (malicious repo code / prompt injection executing *inside* the workspace container), unrestricted egress means a compromised workspace can:

- exfiltrate repo contents, minted git credentials, or fetched secrets to any host;
- reach internal/LAN services the host can see (composes with #23's SSRF, but at the container-network level, not the `fetch`-tool level);
- pull and run arbitrary payloads.

And because there's no credentialed-egress proxy, any workspace tool that legitimately needs an API key currently has to be *given* the key — putting raw durable secrets in the least-trusted place, violating "raw keys never leave the host store." Severity: high for the sandbox's whole reason to exist.

## Proposed change

Two components, designed together:

### 1. Per-workspace egress policy (config + docker wiring)

- Config: `[workspace] egress = "none" | "allowlist" | "full"` as the default, with per-repo overrides later (and per-#53 a repo file may *tighten* it, never loosen).
- Mapping to `docker run`:
  - `none` → `--network none`.
  - `full` → `bridge` (current behaviour, now opt-in).
  - `allowlist` → `--network none` **plus** a route to the broker's egress listener via the existing `--add-host waffle-host:host-gateway` alias (already wired for the provider proxy, `runtime.go:70-73`), and `HTTP(S)_PROXY` env pointing at it so the container's HTTP clients go through the broker.
- Default should be the **restrictive** end for risky contexts (align with #33: cron/group tiers get `none` or `allowlist`, owner-driven workspaces may opt into `full`).

### 2. Broker HTTP egress face

- Authenticate `wk_` tokens (same as the git face).
- Check the session's policy host allowlist (deny-by-default; the allowlist is host config, the trust boundary).
- For an allowlisted host, inject the stored `Authorization` header from the secret store and forward — the container calls `https://api.example.com/…` through the proxy and **never sees the key**.
- Write an audit row per grant/deny, consistent with the git face and provider proxy (`0004_broker_audit.sql`).
- Enforce the same address-class safety as #23 on the proxy's own outbound dials (no proxying to loopback/link-local unless explicitly configured).

## Relationship to #23

#23 hardens the **`fetch` tool** against SSRF (a host-mode and in-tool concern). **This** issue is the **workspace-container network policy + broker egress face** — a different layer (container networking, not a Go tool). They are complementary: #23 protects the host-mode agent; this protects the sandboxed workspace and provides the sanctioned credentialed-egress path. Neither subsumes the other.

### Non-goals

- Not a general forward-proxy for arbitrary protocols — HTTP(S) with header injection is the plan's spec; raw TCP allowlisting is out of scope.
- Not the DNS-level policy (allowlist is by host at the proxy; container `--network none` already blocks non-proxied egress).
- No change to the provider-proxy face's behaviour.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `[workspace] egress` config parses with the three values; per-repo override slot exists (even if only default is wired first). Tested.
- [ ] `egress = "none"` produces `--network none` in the generated `docker run` args (assert on `workspaceRunArgs`, `runtime.go` — already unit-testable); `full` produces `bridge`; `allowlist` produces `--network none` + host alias + proxy env.
- [ ] Broker exposes an HTTP egress endpoint that: rejects unauthenticated/unknown `wk_` tokens; denies hosts not on the session policy allowlist (audit `denied` row); for an allowlisted host, injects the configured `Authorization` header and forwards, returning the upstream response, without the container ever receiving the raw header value.
- [ ] An allowlist-mode workspace can reach an allowlisted test host (via `httptest`) through the proxy and **cannot** reach a non-allowlisted host (two tests).
- [ ] The egress proxy refuses to forward to loopback/link-local/private addresses unless explicitly configured (shares #23's range predicate).
- [ ] Per-grant audit rows are written and are distinguishable from git-face and provider-proxy rows.
- [ ] README/docs document the three tiers, the allowlist config, and the "tool calls an API without holding its key" pattern.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#23 (fetch SSRF):** complementary layer, not a duplicate; the address-range predicate should be shared code.
- **#33 (trust tiering):** egress tier is part of a group's posture — cron/group default to `none`/`allowlist`.
- **#53 (repo policy file):** may tighten egress for its repo, never loosen.
- **#40 (git App tokens):** both are broker faces; consistent audit + auth patterns.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Per-workspace egress policy (none/allowlist/full) and the broker's HTTP egress face are unimplemented: every workspace container gets unrestricted outbound network

## Requirement

docs/plan.md, "Security posture": "**Group chats: sandboxed, restricted tool policy, mention-gated.**" Three properties, none present.

## Current behaviour

The Telegram adapter and gateway treat every chat identically, with no notion of private vs. group:

- `internal/channel/telegram/telegram.go` — the update handler reads `Chat.ID` and `From` but never inspects `Chat.Type` (Telegram sends `"private"` | `"group"` | `"supergroup"` | `"channel"`). `channel.Message` (`internal/channel/channel.go`) carries no group flag, so nothing downstream *can* branch on chat type. A repo-wide grep for "mention" finds nothing.
- `internal/gateway/gateway.go:149-164` — identity check: owner → full processing; anyone else → unconditional pairing-code reply (`"waffle here. I only talk to my owner.\nPairing code: …"`), sent into whatever chat the message came from.

## Failure scenarios

When the bot is added to a group (a normal thing to do with a Telegram bot):

1. **Owner's every group message is processed as if it were a private DM.** No mention required, full tool access (host `bash` under the default config — see #33), so the agent responds to *every* line the owner types in that group, burns tokens on each, and posts its replies where all members see them. The owner cannot participate in the group without triggering the agent.
2. **Every non-owner who speaks gets a pairing code broadcast into the group.** Each unrecognized sender hits the `Pair` path (`gateway.go:156-162`) and the bot replies, in the group, with a live pairing code and host instructions. The code is only redeemable on the host (`waffle pair approve`), so it's not a takeover vector — but it is spam, it's confusing, and it trains group members that the bot answers strangers. In an active group this is a reply per participant per first-contact.

## Impact

The bot is unsafe and antisocial to add to any group today: it over-processes owner messages (cost + noise + host-level tool exposure in a multi-party context), and it spams pairing codes at everyone else. There is no configuration to make it behave; the chat-type signal it would need never reaches the gateway. Severity: medium (no credential compromise, but real cost/exposure/UX failure and a documented posture entirely unmet).

## Proposed change

1. **Surface chat type.** Extend `channel.Message` with `IsGroup bool` (or a `ChatType` enum) and populate it in the Telegram adapter from `Chat.Type`. This is the enabling change everything else needs.
2. **Mention-gate group processing.** In a group, route to the agent **only** when the bot is @-mentioned (or replied-to). Telegram marks mentions via message `entities` of type `mention`/`text_mention`; parse those against the bot's own username (fetch once via `getMe`). Owner messages in a group without a mention are ignored like anyone else's — the owner opts in per-message by mentioning the bot.
3. **DM-only pairing.** Pairing stays a private-chat flow. In a group, non-owner messages are **silently ignored** (no pairing reply). Pairing codes are never emitted into a group.
4. **Restricted tier for group sessions.** Route mention-gated group sessions through the restricted/ sandboxed policy from #33 (a group is a "risky context": multiple untrusted participants). Until #33 lands, at minimum deny host `bash` for group-originated sessions.
5. **Interim safety:** until this ships, document in README that the bot should not be added to group chats.

### Non-goals

- No Telegram admin/permission modeling (who in the group may command the bot) beyond owner-vs-not; a follow-up could allow an allowlist of group members.
- No Discord/other adapters (they don't exist yet; the abstraction added to `channel.Message` should be adapter-neutral so they inherit it).
- Not the general per-group policy engine — that's #33; this issue *consumes* it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `channel.Message` carries a group/chat-type signal, populated by the Telegram adapter from `Chat.Type`; unit test over a group update and a private update.
- [ ] In a group, a message that does **not** mention the bot produces no agent run and no reply (test), for owner and non-owner alike.
- [ ] In a group, a message that **does** mention the bot routes to the agent (test), and the mention token is stripped/handled so it doesn't pollute the prompt.
- [ ] Non-owner messages in a group never produce a pairing-code reply (test); pairing replies still occur in private chats (regression test).
- [ ] Group-originated agent sessions use the restricted policy (no host `bash`), verified against the resulting toolbox — coordinated with #33's mechanism (or a standalone restriction if #33 hasn't landed).
- [ ] Bot username resolution (for mention matching) is fetched/cached, not hardcoded; test uses a stub `getMe`.
- [ ] README documents the group posture (and, until merged, the "don't add to groups" caveat is removed once this lands).

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#33 (per-agent-group trust tiering):** provides the restricted policy this routes group sessions through; ideally lands first, but the mention-gating and pairing fixes are independently shippable.
- **#43 (spend limits):** group chats multiply untrusted senders; per-tier budgets matter more here.
- **#66 (action-level policy):** mention-gating is an event-level rule; a richer policy engine could express it, but a purpose-built gate is the right default.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Group-chat posture unimplemented: Telegram adapter has no chat-type distinction, no mention gating, no restricted policy — the bot processes and spams group traffic

## Requirement

docs/plan.md states this three times, and once as a warning about the cost of *not* doing it early:

- Design principle 4: "Trust still tiers by *session*: the owner's interactive sessions run tools on the host; **risky contexts — repo workspaces, scheduled jobs — run in sandboxes with explicit tool policies**."
- "Decisions to make now", bullet 1: "**agent groups carry `sandbox: host|docker` and a tool allow/deny list from day one**, even while Docker support is unimplemented — retrofitting policy is much harder."
- "Scheduling": "Jobs run as normal (**sandboxed**) sessions."

## Status: partially implemented (core landed)

A first slice landed in PR #74 (commit `084d613`):

- **Config** — `[agent.group.<name>]` sections carry `sandbox` (host|docker) and `tools.allow`/`tools.deny`. `Config.AgentPolicy(group)` resolves a group's effective posture: an explicit group wins; otherwise the global `[sandbox]` applies, except the unattended `cron` group **defaults to denying host `bash`**.
- **buildAgent** is parameterized by agent group and builds its executor + tool policy from the resolved posture (`chat`/`selfdev` use `main`).
- **serve** builds two agents — a `main` agent for the gateway and a restricted `cron` agent for the scheduler — which **no longer share one Agent**. A cron prompt can't reach host shell by default.
- Tests: `AgentPolicy` defaults + explicit-group override; `buildAgent` yields a cron toolbox without `bash` and a main toolbox with it.

### Still open (follow-up, tracked here)

- [ ] **Per-session dynamic group routing inside the gateway** — distinct Telegram groups → distinct policies, resolved per session and surviving a store round-trip. `entity.AgentGroup` is still hardcoded to `"main"` for channel sessions. This composes with #34 (group-chat posture), which introduces the non-`main` group concept; best done alongside it.
- [ ] **Persist the resolved policy with the session** so the gateway enforces it per-session across restarts (depends on the routing above).
- [ ] **docker executor reliability** for `sandbox = "docker"` on non-linux hosts is handled by #42 (linux runner) — the restricted-host-policy tier is the usable default until then.

## Current behaviour (original finding, for reference)

- `internal/config/config.go` — previously a single global `[sandbox]` section and one global tool policy; nothing keyed by agent group.
- `internal/entity/entity.go` — `g.AgentGroup = "main"` hardcoded.
- `cmd/waffle/serve_cmd.go` — one shared `Agent` served both the gateway and the cron `schedule.Runner`, so scheduled jobs executed host tools exactly like the owner's chat.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Config supports `[agent.group.<name>]` with `sandbox` and `tools.allow`/`tools.deny`; parsing tested incl. unknown-group fallback to the documented default.
- [x] A session created for the `cron` group resolves to that group's policy; a session for `main` resolves to its own — asserted by building both and inspecting the resulting toolbox.
- [x] By default (no `[agent.group.cron]`), a scheduled job's toolbox **excludes host `bash`** (test).
- [x] `serve` no longer passes one shared `Agent` to both gateway and scheduler.
- [x] Existing single-`[sandbox]` configs keep working; the cron behaviour change is documented (README).
- [ ] The gateway resolves per-session policy from the session's agent group, surviving a store round-trip. *(follow-up — see above)*
- [ ] The resolved policy persists with the session. *(follow-up)*

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#43 (spend/rate limits):** per-group budgets attach to this policy layer.
- **#44 (memory/skill write gate):** "restrict `remember`/`distill_skill` in risky contexts" is a per-group tool-policy entry that now has a home.
- **#34 (group-chat posture):** provides the non-`main` group concept the deferred gateway routing needs; do the per-session routing there.
- **#42 (linux runner):** makes `sandbox = "docker"` honest on non-linux; the restricted-host tier is the default until docker mode is set up.
- **#53 (repo policy file):** repo files may *tighten* a group's grant, never loosen it — this issue defines the authoritative layer.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; core implemented in PR #74. File:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Per-agent-group trust tiering unimplemented: one global sandbox mode and tool policy, so scheduled jobs run tools on the host exactly like the owner's interactive chat

## Requirement

docs/plan.md, "Secret management": the broker "authenticates callers with per-session `wk_` tokens **and applies the session's policy**", and its git face "mints short-lived, least-privilege repo credentials … **scoped to the single repo**, ~1 h TTL". The stated threat model is explicit: "a fully compromised session … **cannot read another repo**, another session's secrets, or any raw key." The plan permits a fine-grained PAT as the first-iteration fallback for the *minting* half — but never for skipping the *policy* half.

## Current behaviour

The git-credential face authenticates the session token but then ignores both the session identity and the requested repo path when deciding what to return:

- `cmd/waffle/ws_cmd.go:157-173` — `gitCredentialFromSecrets` takes `(ctx, sessionID, host, path)` and uses **only** `host`: `if host != "github.com" { ... }`, then returns the owner's stored fine-grained PAT (`secret://github/token` / `GITHUB_TOKEN`) verbatim as `x-access-token`. `sessionID` and `path` are unread.
- `internal/broker/broker.go:167-185` — `serveGitCredential` authenticates the `wk_` token, resolves it to a session, and passes `sessionID` and `path` through to the func — but nothing between the token check and the credential return enforces that the session is *entitled* to that repo.
- The binding needed to enforce scope **already exists**: the workspaces table stores the session↔repo link (`internal/workspace/workspace.go`, the `Workspace{SessionID, Repo}` row), so the check is a lookup, not new plumbing.

## Failure scenario

1. Session S is opened for repo `owner/A` (`waffle ws open owner/A` → mints `wk_S`, container gets it as `WAFFLE_SESSION_TOKEN`).
2. Malicious code in repo A (or a prompt injection driving the agent inside that sandbox — the plan's own threat model) issues a git operation against `owner/B`, or calls the broker's credential endpoint directly with `path=owner/B`.
3. The broker authenticates `wk_S` (valid), calls `gitCredentialFromSecrets`, which returns the **full PAT** — a durable credential with access to *every* repo the PAT can see.
4. The compromised session now has push/pull to `owner/B`, other private repos, everything the PAT covers. The "cannot read another repo" property is violated with a single request.

The PAT is not just over-scoped — it is a *raw durable credential* handed to the least-trusted component, which also violates the broker's "raw keys never leave the host store" rule.

## Impact

Direct violation of the broker's core security contract, exploitable by exactly the actor the sandbox exists to contain. Severity: high. This is the policy-enforcement half; #40 is the token-minting half (short TTL, GitHub-side scoping). They compose but are independently valuable — **this one closes the cross-repo hole with the existing PAT and no new dependencies**, so it should land first.

## Proposed change

1. In the `GitCredentialFunc` wired by `ws`/`serve`, before returning any credential: resolve `sessionID → workspace → repo` (workspace store lookup) and **refuse** (`return "", "", err`) when the requested `path` does not match that session's bound repo. Deny-by-default: a session with no workspace binding (e.g. a plain chat session) gets no git credential.
2. Normalize the comparison carefully: `path` from git's credential protocol may arrive as `owner/repo`, `owner/repo.git`, with or without a leading slash — canonicalize both sides before comparing, and test the variants (a sloppy match is a bypass).
3. Emit an audit row on denial (`denied`, with session, requested path, bound repo) using the existing broker audit path (`internal/store/migrations/0004_broker_audit.sql`), so cross-repo attempts are visible.
4. Keep returning the PAT on a **match** (that's #40's job to improve); this issue only adds the gate.

### Non-goals

- Not the short-TTL installation-token backend — that's #40.
- No change to the provider-proxy face or the (unbuilt) egress face.
- No per-file-path scoping within a repo (repo granularity matches the plan).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A session bound to repo A requesting credentials for repo B receives an error (git sees an auth failure), no credential is returned, and a `denied` audit row is written naming the session, requested path, and bound repo.
- [ ] A session bound to repo A requesting credentials for repo A succeeds (regression: the happy path still works end to end).
- [ ] A session with **no** workspace binding requesting any repo is denied (deny-by-default), with an audit row.
- [ ] Path canonicalization is covered by tests: `owner/A`, `/owner/A`, `owner/A.git`, `owner/a` (case) all resolve consistently against a binding for `owner/A`, and none of the variants lets `owner/B` through.
- [ ] Host mismatch (`host != github.com`) still refused as today (regression).
- [ ] The audit row schema/fields are consistent with the existing broker audit rows (grant vs. deny distinguishable).
- [ ] Tests use a fake credential func / in-memory workspace store — no live GitHub calls.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#40 (GitHub App installation tokens):** the minting half. An installation token's `repositories:` field enforces scope at GitHub's side too, so #40 + this issue give defense in depth (broker refuses B *and* the token couldn't touch B even if it leaked). #40's design should call this func's post-#32 signature.
- **#33 (per-agent-group policy):** the general "apply the session's policy" mechanism; this is the specific git-face instance of it.
- **#48 (ws races serve):** note the token map is in-memory per process (`Broker.tokens`) — this check must resolve the binding from the **store**, not from whichever process happens to hold the token, or #48's race reintroduces the hole. Call this out in the implementation.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Broker git-credential face ignores session→repo scope: any valid wk_ token retrieves the full durable PAT for any repository

## Motivation

The sandbox IPC design puts a pair of SQLite databases (`inbound.db`/`outbound.db`) on a host directory that is bind-mounted into the container (`internal/sandbox/docker.go:98` — `-v <QueueDir>:/waffle/queue`), with the host and the in-container runner both opening them concurrently. SQLite's correctness under concurrency rests on two filesystem guarantees: POSIX advisory locks that actually exclude across all writers, and `fsync` that actually orders writes. On Linux with a local filesystem both hold. On macOS Docker Desktop, the bind mount crosses a VM boundary through a file-sharing layer (VirtioFS today, gRPC-FUSE historically), and **SQLite's own documentation warns against multi-process SQLite over network/shared filesystems for exactly this reason** — lock semantics across such layers are historically incomplete.

This issue is deliberately scoped as *risk to verify*, not *bug to fix*: the failure would be intermittent and environment-specific, and the codebase's own comments show the queue was designed assuming same-kernel semantics.

## Current behaviour

- `internal/sandbox/queue.go:63-71` — both sides open the DBs with `journal_mode(TRUNCATE)`, `busy_timeout(5000)`, `synchronous(FULL)`. TRUNCATE journaling (not WAL — correctly, since WAL requires shared memory that definitely does not cross the mount) means every commit depends on honored exclusive locks and honored fsync.
- `internal/sandbox/docker.go:98` — the queue dir crosses into the container as a bind mount; the host writes tool requests into `inbound.db`, the runner polls it, writes results/heartbeats into `outbound.db`, and the host polls that (`internal/sandbox/client.go`, `runner.go`).
- Host platform for the deployment that motivated this: **darwin** (Docker Desktop mediates every byte of the mount through the Linux VM's file-sharing daemon).

## Failure modes to look for

1. **Lock passthrough failure** → concurrent host `INSERT` and runner `SELECT/UPDATE` interleave without exclusion → `SQLITE_BUSY` storms past the 5 s busy_timeout, or silent lost updates.
2. **Stale page cache across the boundary** → the host reads an outdated `outbound.db` → heartbeats appear missing → false "runner appears dead" teardown (the 10 s heartbeat window in the client), or results that were written but never observed.
3. **fsync not honored through the VM layer** → post-crash journal replay sees torn state → real database corruption after an ungraceful stop.

Symptoms would present as the sandbox flakiness bugs this repo has already chased (dead-runner detection, undelivered results — cf. the fixed #5/#13/#14 lineage), which is precisely why a targeted reproduction is worth doing before more tuning of timeouts.

## What would confirm or clear it

- [x] A reproduction harness: a Go test (or script) that runs the real queue pair over a Docker Desktop bind mount and hammers both sides (host goroutine inserting requests, containerized runner consuming, for N minutes), asserting: no `SQLITE_BUSY` beyond busy_timeout, every request gets exactly one result, heartbeat gaps never exceed the poll interval ×2.
- [x] A crash test: `docker kill` mid-write, then integrity-check both DBs (`PRAGMA integrity_check`).
- [x] A documentation check: current Docker Desktop/VirtioFS statements on POSIX lock and fsync passthrough (VirtioFS has materially improved since gRPC-FUSE; the risk may be historical). Record findings either way.

## Resolution paths (pick based on findings)

- **Cleared:** document "queue over bind mount is supported on Docker Desktop ≥ version X (VirtioFS)" in README plus a note in `queue.go`, and close.
- **Confirmed:** move the queue off the shared filesystem. Ranked options: (a) TCP/Unix-socket transport to the host (the broker already demonstrates the host-listener pattern with `--add-host waffle-host:host-gateway`, `internal/workspace/runtime.go:70-73`); (b) single-writer-per-file protocol (each side only ever writes its own DB, eliminating cross-boundary lock contention — closest to current code); (c) named volume + `docker exec` relay. Whichever is chosen supersedes this issue with a concrete implementation issue.
- Either way: `waffle doctor` gains a sandbox-queue probe (start a throwaway container, exercise one request/response round trip) so environment regressions are caught by the existing self-check machinery — composes with #42's proposed docker probe.

### Non-goals

- No switch to WAL (impossible across the boundary: WAL's shm requirement).
- No general rearchitecture of the sandbox protocol beyond what the findings force.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] The reproduction harness exists in-tree (build-tagged or opt-in via env var so CI on Linux isn't blocked by it) and its README section documents how to run it on a macOS host.
- [x] Findings are recorded on this issue: pass/fail per failure mode, Docker Desktop + VirtioFS version tested.
- [x] The outcome is one of: (a) documented support statement + close; or (b) a follow-up implementation issue for the chosen transport, with this issue closed as superseded by it.
- [x] `waffle doctor` includes a sandbox round-trip check when docker mode is configured, reported like the existing checks (`internal/selfdev/selfdev.go:50-88` `add(...)` pattern).

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#42 (host-OS binary bind-mounted):** on macOS the runner currently can't start at all, which *masks* this issue — #42 must be fixed before the reproduction can even run. Sequence: #42 → this.
- **#64 (queue identity is connection-local):** any transport replacement chosen here must preserve/implement #64's durable-identity requirements; coordinate the designs.
- **#46 (resource limits):** unrelated mechanically, but the same `docker run` arg builders will be touched; rebase order only.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Sandbox SQLite queue over a Docker bind mount depends on cross-VM advisory locks and fsync: unverified on macOS Docker Desktop (needs reproduction)

## Problem
Chat command dispatch uses `strings.HasPrefix(line, "/skill")` and `strings.HasPrefix(line, "/repo")` with no word boundary, so ordinary input that merely starts with those bytes is misrouted into skill/workspace handling.

## Where
- `cmd/waffle/chat_cmd.go:120` — `case strings.HasPrefix(line, "/skill"):`
- `cmd/waffle/chat_cmd.go:126` — `case strings.HasPrefix(line, "/repo"):`

## Impact
`/report the bug` matches `/repo` → `TrimPrefix` yields `"rt the bug"` → tries to open a bogus workspace and errors. `/skills` matches `/skill` → routes into `skillMessage("s")` → "unknown skill". No crash, but normal-ish input is hijacked. UX-level correctness bug.

## Proposed solution
Require a word boundary: match the exact command or command-plus-space, e.g. `line == "/repo" || strings.HasPrefix(line, "/repo ")` (same for `/skill`), or tokenize the leading word and switch on it. Add tests for `/report`, `/skills`, and the valid forms.
title: /skill and /repo use prefix matching and misroute inputs like /report and /skills

## Problem
`memory.Append` dates notes with `time.Now().Format("2006-01-02")` in **local** time, while sessions/entities/jobs persist timestamps in UTC (`time.Now().UTC()`). Near midnight, a note lands under a different calendar day than the UTC-stamped turn history it accompanies.

## Where
- `internal/memory/memory.go:82` — `time.Now().Format("2006-01-02")` (local)
- Contrast: `internal/session/session.go:40` — `time.Now().UTC().Format(...)`; `internal/workspace/workspace.go:109` uses the same UTC helper.

## Impact
Low severity / cosmetic: MEMORY.md note dates can disagree by a day with the searchable turn history for the same conversation, and near-midnight notes land under the "wrong" day relative to UTC.

## Proposed solution
Use `time.Now().UTC().Format("2006-01-02")` for consistency with the rest of the store (or route all timestamping through the shared `now()` helper). Good first issue.
title: memory notes are dated in local time while the rest of the store uses UTC

body:
## Problem
Concurrent-`Open` reconciliation depends on matching driver error-message substrings: `strings.Contains(err, "unique constraint failed") && (Contains "workspaces.repo" || Contains "idx_workspaces_repo_active")`. If `modernc.org/sqlite`'s wording changes across versions (a partial index's message can name the index rather than the column), the match returns false and the race is mishandled.

## Where
- `internal/workspace/workspace.go:301-310` — `isUniqueConstraintError`
- `internal/workspace/workspace.go:204-216` — call site: on a false negative it tears down the loser's container/volume/session (already done at :204-207) and returns the raw error at :216 instead of resuming the winner.

## Impact
A benign concurrent-`Open` race becomes a user-visible failure whenever the driver's message doesn't contain the expected substrings. No test pins the wording and there is no fallback, so it's a fragile, version-dependent assumption (works in practice today with current modernc wording).

## Proposed solution
Detect the constraint violation structurally rather than by full-message substring: use `modernc.org/sqlite`'s typed error / result code (`SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE`, code 2067) via `errors.As`, falling back to a case-insensitive "unique constraint failed" check without requiring the column/index name. Add a test that forces the partial-index violation and asserts reconciliation resumes the winner.
title: Fragile driver-string-based unique-constraint detection in workspace race reconciliation

## Motivation

FTS5 external-content tables hold **no copy of the text** — they index rowids into the content table and require the application to mirror every `DELETE`/`UPDATE` into the index, conventionally via triggers. Get that wrong and the index doesn't degrade gracefully: queries against stale entries return garbage or hard errors ("database disk image is malformed" from `snippet()`/`highlight()` over a vanished rowid). The SQLite documentation is blunt that delete/update synchronization is mandatory for external-content tables.

waffle's schema already contains the delete mechanism (`ON DELETE CASCADE`) but only half the synchronization. Nothing fires today — but #47 (data lifecycle: `session rm`, `forget`, retention) is an open issue whose entire purpose is to add the delete path. The correctness prerequisite should land first, separately, so #47 can't ship subtly broken.

## Current behaviour

`internal/store/migrations/0002_sessions.sql`:

```sql
session_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES sessions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,   -- :13
...
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE turns_fts USING fts5(text, content='turns', content_rowid='id');  -- :22

-- turns are insert-only, so one trigger keeps the index current.       -- :24
CREATE TRIGGER turns_after_insert AFTER INSERT ON turns BEGIN           -- :25-27
    INSERT INTO turns_fts (rowid, text) VALUES (new.id, new.text);
END;
```

The comment records the assumption ("turns are insert-only") — true of the Go code today (no `DELETE FROM sessions` / `DELETE FROM turns` statement exists in the tree), but the **schema itself** already promises cascade deletion, and foreign keys are enabled per connection (`_pragma=foreign_keys(1)`, `internal/store/store.go:36-41`). Any of these breaks the assumption without touching this file:

- #47's `waffle session rm` / retention job (the tracked plan),
- an ad-hoc `sqlite3` cleanup by the operator (the DB is a plain file in `~/.waffle`),
- any future code path that updates `turns.text` (the trigger set doesn't cover `UPDATE` either).

After any of those, `turns_fts` holds rowids pointing at deleted/changed content. Reads via `snippet(turns_fts, …)` (used by session search, `internal/session/session.go`) can return corrupt snippets or raise SQLITE_CORRUPT-class errors — and the corruption is *persistent* in the index until a full rebuild.

## Impact

Latent today, guaranteed the moment a delete path lands. The failure presents as recall/search breakage far from the deletion that caused it, and looks like database corruption (alarming, hard to diagnose, resolved only by `INSERT INTO turns_fts(turns_fts) VALUES('rebuild')`). It also silently blocks #47: a session "deleted" for privacy reasons **remains searchable** via the orphaned FTS entries until the index is fixed — the opposite of what deletion promised.

## Proposed change

A new migration (numbered per the scheme in `internal/store/migrations/`, respecting #24's runner semantics) adding the two standard external-content sync triggers:

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER turns_after_delete AFTER DELETE ON turns BEGIN
    INSERT INTO turns_fts (turns_fts, rowid, text) VALUES ('delete', old.id, old.text);
END;

CREATE TRIGGER turns_after_update AFTER UPDATE ON turns BEGIN
    INSERT INTO turns_fts (turns_fts, rowid, text) VALUES ('delete', old.id, old.text);
    INSERT INTO turns_fts (rowid, text) VALUES (new.id, new.text);
END;
```

Plus, in the same migration, a one-time `INSERT INTO turns_fts(turns_fts) VALUES('rebuild');` — cheap insurance that any index already skewed by out-of-band edits is repaired at upgrade time.

Update the stale comment in `0002_sessions.sql`? No — migrations are immutable once applied; instead the new migration's header comment supersedes it ("turns are no longer assumed insert-only; delete/update are mirrored").

### Non-goals

- Not the delete feature itself — that's #47 (this is its declared prerequisite).
- No schema change to `turns` or `sessions`.
- No switch away from external-content FTS (contentless/regular FTS trade space for this maintenance; the current design is fine once synchronized).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] New migration adds `AFTER DELETE` and `AFTER UPDATE` triggers exactly mirroring the external-content FTS5 sync pattern, plus a one-time index `rebuild`.
- [ ] Test: insert a session with turns, `DELETE FROM sessions WHERE id=…` directly through the store's DB handle, then (a) FTS search for the deleted content returns zero rows, and (b) an FTS5 **integrity-check** (`INSERT INTO turns_fts(turns_fts, rank) VALUES('integrity-check', 1)` in FTS5's external-content mode) passes without error.
- [ ] Test: `UPDATE turns SET text=…` then search finds the new text and not the old.
- [ ] Test: search with `snippet(turns_fts, …)` after a cascade delete neither errors nor returns content from deleted turns.
- [ ] Migration is idempotent under the runner (applies once, recorded once) and passes `doctor`'s migrate-on-snapshot check.
- [ ] The migration's header comment documents why the triggers exist and supersedes the "insert-only" note in 0002.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#47 (data lifecycle):** hard prerequisite; #47's first checklist item should be "land #25".
- **#24 (migration runner set-semantics):** this migration will be assigned the next version number; if #24 hasn't landed, coordinate numbering to avoid the out-of-order trap it describes.
- **#60 (memory retrieval tiers):** any future re-indexing or embedding store should copy this pattern — external-content indexes must ship their sync triggers in the same migration.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: turns_fts is an external-content FTS5 index with only an INSERT trigger: the schema's ON DELETE CASCADE is a loaded gun for the first delete path that lands

## Motivation

The store is the substrate every subsystem persists through (sessions, entities, broker audit, workspaces, jobs — `internal/store/migrations/0001`–`0006`), and several open issues will add migrations of their own (#25's FTS triggers, #47's retention, #55's usage accounting, #67's working set). The migration runner is therefore about to see much more traffic — including parallel branches that each allocate "the next" version number. Its current skip rule turns that ordinary workflow into silent schema divergence: the failure appears far from its cause, at query time, on whichever machine happened to apply migrations in the unlucky order.

## Current behaviour

`migrate` (`internal/store/store.go:116-145`) reads a single high-water mark and skips everything at or below it:

```go
var current sql.NullInt64
db.QueryRowContext(ctx, `SELECT MAX(version) FROM schema_migrations`).Scan(&current)  // store.go:127-128
...
for _, m := range ms {
    if current.Valid && int64(m.version) <= current.Int64 {   // store.go:137
        continue
    }
    ...
}
```

`loadMigrations` (`store.go:88-114`) sorts embedded files and rejects **duplicate** versions (`store.go:109-110`) but is silent about **gaps**.

The failure sequence:

1. Branch A adds `0007_foo.sql`, merges, its binary runs → `schema_migrations` has max 7.
2. Branch B (cut earlier) adds `0006_late.sql`, merges afterward.
3. Next startup: `0006 <= 7` → skipped. It is **not applied** and **not recorded** — `schema_migrations` has no row for 6, so nothing ever flags the omission.
4. First query touching `0006`'s table/column fails at runtime: `no such table: …`, on whatever code path happens to hit it first, possibly days later, possibly only on one machine.

Two machines that applied the same set of migration files in different merge orders now have **different schemas** with identical version high-water marks — the worst kind of divergence, because `doctor`'s "database migrates" check (`internal/selfdev/selfdev.go:66-73`, which runs `migrate` against a snapshot) also passes on both.

## Impact

Silent, permanent schema divergence triggered by a completely normal git workflow (two branches, out-of-order merge). Detection is delayed to an unrelated runtime error; recovery requires manual forensics (diff `schema_migrations` against the embedded set). Severity: high for a project that upgrades itself from git refs (`waffle upgrade` checks out arbitrary refs — version-number ordering across refs is exactly the hazard).

## Proposed change

Track applied migrations as a **set**, not a high-water mark:

1. `migrate` reads `SELECT version FROM schema_migrations` into a `map[int]bool` and applies any embedded migration whose version is absent — regardless of order.
2. **Fail fast on retrograde application where order matters:** applying a migration whose version is *lower* than the current max is only safe if migrations are independent. Since SQLite migrations here do sometimes build on prior schema, make the policy explicit and strict: apply the missing migration **and log a prominent warning** naming it as out-of-order — or, stricter, refuse to start with an error instructing the operator to verify (`migration 0006 is older than already-applied 0007; applying out of order`). Pick one, document it in the code, test it. Recommendation: apply-with-warning — refusing bricks startup for a case that is usually safe, and the warning creates the audit trail.
3. Keep the duplicate-version rejection in `loadMigrations`; additionally reject a **gap in the embedded set** (e.g. files 1,2,4) at load time — embedded files are fully under our control, so a gap there is always a packaging mistake.
4. `doctor`'s migrate-on-snapshot check inherits all of this for free (it calls the same path).

### Non-goals

- No checksum/content-hash verification of already-applied migrations (valuable, but a separate hardening; this issue is about the skip rule).
- No down-migrations.
- No renumbering of existing migrations 0001–0006.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `migrate` applies every embedded migration whose version is not present in `schema_migrations`, including versions lower than the current max; each application inserts its row.
- [ ] Test: apply `{1,2,4}` (simulate branch A), then add `3` to the embedded set and re-run `migrate` → `3` is applied, recorded, and its schema objects exist (query them).
- [ ] Test: re-running `migrate` on a fully applied set is a no-op (idempotence preserved).
- [ ] Out-of-order application emits the documented warning (or error, if the strict policy is chosen) naming the migration — asserted in the test.
- [ ] `loadMigrations` rejects an embedded set with a version gap, with an error naming the missing number (test).
- [ ] Duplicate-version rejection still covered by test.
- [ ] The `applyOne` transaction semantics are unchanged: a failing migration applies nothing and records nothing (existing behaviour, add a regression test if none exists).
- [ ] A comment on `migrate` documents the set-based rule and the out-of-order policy so the next migration author doesn't have to re-derive it.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#25 (FTS triggers migration) and #47/#55/#67 (each adds migrations):** all become safer to develop on parallel branches once this lands; land this first.
- **#45 (backup/restore):** restore + upgrade across versions exercises exactly this runner; the set-based rule makes restore-then-migrate deterministic.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Migration runner compares against MAX(version) only: an out-of-order migration is skipped forever, unrecorded, and surfaces later as runtime "no such table"

## Motivation

docs/plan.md's security posture treats all fetched content as untrusted data ("never as instructions"), and its designated network control for risky contexts is a **policy-gated egress proxy per workspace** (docs/plan.md, "Repo workspaces": egress "none / allowlist via host egress proxy / full"). That control does not exist yet (#35 tracks it). Until it does, the `fetch` tool is the agent's unrestricted network arm — and it is reachable from every context that has the builtin toolbox, including sandboxed sessions whose *other* boundaries were built precisely because their inputs are untrusted.

SSRF via an LLM tool is not hypothetical: a fetched page containing "now fetch http://169.254.169.254/…" is the canonical indirect-prompt-injection escalation, because the *response body is returned into the model's context*, completing the exfiltration loop in one round trip.

## Current behaviour

`Fetch.Run` (`internal/tool/builtin.go:232-264`) validates only the scheme:

```go
if !strings.HasPrefix(in.URL, "http://") && !strings.HasPrefix(in.URL, "https://") {
    return "", fmt.Errorf("only http(s) URLs are supported, got %q", in.URL)
}
```

then performs a plain `http.DefaultClient.Do(req)` GET (`builtin.go:250`). No resolution check, no IP-range policy, no redirect re-validation (`http.DefaultClient` follows up to 10 redirects, each to an unchecked destination). The response is returned to the model (bounded to `OutputLimit`, `builtin.go:263`); it is not a stored secret, so `secret.Redactor` never touches it.

Reachable targets today, from any session with `fetch`:

- `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/…` — cloud IMDS, live credentials, on any cloud-hosted deployment.
- `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` — anything listening on the host's loopback, **including waffle's own credential broker** (`[broker] listen`, e.g. `127.0.0.1:8421`). Broker endpoints require a `wk_` bearer token, so this is probing rather than theft — but the SSRF turns "loopback-only, therefore trusted-caller-only" into a false assumption.
- RFC1918 / link-local addresses: internal dashboards, printers, routers, unauthenticated admin planes.
- DNS-rebind variants: a hostname that resolves publicly at check time and to `127.0.0.1` at dial time defeats any naive pre-resolution check.

## Impact

In host mode the operator is trusted, but the *content* driving the model is not — the plan's own threat model. A single injected instruction in any fetched page or inbound message can read IMDS credentials or map the host's loopback/LAN, with results delivered straight back into the transcript (and, via `remember` — see #44 — potentially persisted). Defense-in-depth gap of moderate severity now, high severity for any cloud-hosted or LAN-attached deployment.

## Proposed change

Two tracks, explicitly ordered:

### Track 1 (this issue): resolution-aware guard inside `fetch`

1. Add a custom `http.Transport` whose `DialContext` resolves the host and **checks the actual IP being dialed** (not a separate pre-resolution pass — this is what defeats DNS rebinding): reject loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`), link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, `fe80::/10`), unspecified, and private ranges (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, `fc00::/7`) using `netip.Addr` predicates.
2. Apply the same check on **every redirect hop** via `CheckRedirect` (or simply rely on the dial-time check, which covers redirects for free — document which).
3. Config escape hatch for legitimate local use: `[tools.fetch] allow_private = ["192.168.1.0/24", "localhost:3000"]` — explicit allowlist entries, empty by default. Config is the trust boundary per plan principle 7.
4. Clear tool-facing error: `fetch: refused: <ip> is in a private/link-local range; add it to [tools.fetch] allow_private if intended` — the model can relay it intelligibly.

### Track 2 (tracked by #35, not this issue): the real control

The per-workspace egress policy and the broker's HTTP egress face. When #35 lands, sandboxed `fetch` traffic should route through the proxy; the in-tool guard stays as the host-mode and belt-and-braces layer.

### Non-goals

- No general URL allowlisting or content filtering — only address-class policy.
- No change to the 2 MiB body cap, 30 s timeout, or output truncation (`builtin.go:242,258,263`).
- Not the sandbox network story (`--network none` already exists for sandbox mode; workspaces are #35).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fetch` of a URL whose host resolves to loopback, link-local (including `169.254.169.254`), unspecified, or RFC1918/ULA ranges fails with the documented error, by default, in both host and sandbox toolboxes.
- [ ] The check happens at **dial time** on the connected address: a test with a custom resolver (or a hosts-file-style stub) that returns a public IP at first resolution and `127.0.0.1` at dial time still gets refused (DNS-rebind regression test).
- [ ] A redirect from an allowed public URL to a private address is refused (test with `httptest` server issuing a 302 to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`).
- [ ] `[tools.fetch] allow_private` entries (CIDR and host:port forms) permit exactly the listed destinations; an empty/absent config permits none (tests for both).
- [ ] IPv6 equivalents are covered (`::1`, `fe80::/10`, `fc00::/7`) — at minimum unit tests over the range predicate.
- [ ] The refusal error names the resolved IP and the config key; no partial response body is ever returned on refusal.
- [ ] Existing `TestFetch` (`internal/tool/tool_test.go:106`) keeps passing — note it uses an `httptest` loopback server, so the test toolbox must opt in via the allowlist mechanism (this doubles as the allowlist test).
- [ ] README/docs note the new default and the escape hatch.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#35 (egress policy + broker HTTP face):** the designated long-term control; this issue is the defense-in-depth layer that must not wait for it. The config introduced here should be designed so #35's per-workspace policy can subsume it.
- **#44 (memory writes as persistence channel):** SSRF output → `remember` is the escalation chain that turns a one-shot fetch into standing state; both guards shrink it independently.
- **#66 (action-level tool policy):** a rules engine could express this as policy; until then the guard is hardcoded in the tool, which is the right default anyway.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: fetch has no loopback/link-local/private-range guard (SSRF): prompt-injected content can read cloud metadata and internal services until the egress proxy exists

## Problem
The `write_file` tool creates files at mode `0o644` (world-readable). Agents are routinely asked to write secret-bearing content (tokens, keys, config), and this contrasts with the rest of the codebase, which deliberately hardens permissions (`store` uses `0o700` dirs, `secret/filestore` writes `0o600`).

## Where
- `internal/tool/builtin.go:148` — `os.WriteFile(in.Path, []byte(in.Content), 0o644)`
- Contrast: `internal/store/store.go:32` (`0o700`), `internal/secret/filestore.go:85` (`0o600`)
- Note: `edit_file` already correctly *preserves* the existing file mode via `info.Mode().Perm()`.

## Impact
On a shared/multi-user host, secret-bearing content written via `write_file` lands world-readable — every local user can read it. Low severity (arbitrary-path write itself is intended under the host-trust model), but the default permission is a genuine, easy hardening win.

## Proposed solution
Default new `write_file` files to `0o600`. If a broader default is wanted for non-secret output, honor the process umask or an explicit mode arg — but the safe default should be owner-only, matching the rest of the tree.
title: write_file creates world-readable (0o644) files; default to 0o600

## Problem
`selfdev` runs `git checkout <ref>` with the ref as a bare argument and no `--` separator, so a ref beginning with `-` is parsed by git as an option (classic argument injection). Because the upgrade flow then builds and executes the result, a hostile ref could escalate toward code execution.

## Where
- `internal/selfdev/selfdev.go:111` — `run(ctx, repoDir, stderr, "git", "checkout", ref)` (no `--`)
- ref origin: `cmd/waffle/selfdev_cmd.go:55-57` (`ref = args[0]`) → `:77` `selfdev.Upgrade(...)`

## Impact
Low today: `ref` is operator-supplied via the local CLI, and per the trust model the operator already has host shell. It becomes meaningful only if an agent-driven self-dev path (envisioned in docs/plan.md) can influence the ref that reaches `Upgrade`. Worth fixing as defense-in-depth.

## Proposed solution
Insert an explicit end-of-options separator: `git checkout -- <ref>` (or use `git switch --detach <ref>` with validation), and reject refs starting with `-`. Apply the same pattern to any other place a ref/branch flows into a git argument. Trivial fix — good first issue.
title: git checkout uses an unvalidated ref without '--' separator (option injection in upgrade path)

## Motivation

`waffle cron add` is the command that configures **unattended** work: once a job is stored, nobody is watching when it fires. A parsing bug at add-time therefore doesn't surface as an error — it surfaces days later as a job that ran, produced output, and delivered it nowhere (results default to logs when `deliver` is empty, `cmd/waffle/cron_cmd.go:115-120`). Misconfiguration of unattended jobs must fail loudly at the only moment a human is present: the `add` command.

## Current behaviour

`splitDeliver` (`cmd/waffle/cron_cmd.go:122-132`):

```go
func splitDeliver(args []string) (fields []string, deliver string) {
    for i := 0; i < len(args); i++ {
        if args[i] == "--deliver" && i+1 < len(args) {
            deliver = args[i+1]
            i++
            continue
        }
        fields = append(fields, args[i])
    }
    return fields, deliver
}
```

The `i+1 < len(args)` guard means a **trailing** `--deliver` with no value doesn't error — it falls through to the append and the literal string `"--deliver"` becomes an ordinary field. Downstream, `prompt := joinFields(fields[6:])` (`cron_cmd.go:53`) folds it into the stored prompt.

Concretely:

```
waffle cron add standup 0 9 * * 1-5 "Summarize my starred repos" --deliver
```

creates a job with:
- `Prompt` = `Summarize my starred repos --deliver` — the flag leaks into the text the model receives every firing;
- `Deliver` = `""` — results go to the serve log only, not to Telegram.

A second, adjacent hazard in the same function: `--deliver` consumes whatever token follows it with no shape validation, so `--deliver "do the thing"` (value forgotten, prompt word swallowed) stores a garbage delivery target that only fails at delivery time — `ParseTarget` (`internal/schedule/schedule.go:322`) returns `ok=false` at fire time, again silently downgrading to log-only.

## Impact

A silently misconfigured unattended job instead of a loud add-time error. The user believes they'll get a Telegram message every weekday at 09:00; instead the output lands in a log they aren't reading, and the prompt itself is polluted with a stray `--deliver` token. Severity: low (operator-only surface, no security dimension) but disproportionately annoying because the failure is deferred and quiet.

## Proposed change

1. **Trailing flag is a usage error.** `splitDeliver` returns an error when `--deliver` is the last token: `--deliver requires a value (channel:chat_id, e.g. telegram:900)`.
2. **Validate the value's shape at add-time.** After splitting, run the value through the existing `schedule.ParseTarget` and reject values it cannot parse — the parser already exists and is the exact predicate delivery will apply later. (Validating channel *existence* is out of scope; shape only.)
3. Return the usage error before `jobs.Add` is called — nothing is persisted on a parse failure.

### Non-goals

- No new flag framework; keep the hand-rolled scan, just make it total over its input space.
- No re-validation of already-stored jobs (a one-off `cron ls` eyeball covers the installed base; there is no migration need).
- `--deliver` appearing more than once can keep last-wins semantics (or error — implementer's choice), as long as it is tested and deliberate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `waffle cron add <name> <5 cron fields> <prompt> --deliver` (trailing, no value) exits non-zero with a usage error that names the flag and the expected value shape; **no job row is created** (assert via `jobs.List`).
- [ ] `--deliver telegram:900` in any position (before or after the prompt words) still parses: prompt excludes the flag pair, `Deliver == "telegram:900"`.
- [ ] A `--deliver` value that `schedule.ParseTarget` rejects (e.g. `--deliver banana`) is a add-time usage error, not a stored job.
- [ ] The stored prompt never contains the literal token `--deliver` in any accepted invocation (test asserts on the persisted `Job.Prompt`).
- [ ] Unit tests (table-driven) for `splitDeliver` cover: no flag; flag mid-args; flag last-with-value; flag trailing-without-value; value that fails `ParseTarget`; flag given twice.
- [ ] `cron add` usage text (`cronUsage`, `cron_cmd.go:100-113`) documents the `channel:chat_id` shape (it already shows an example; keep it in sync with the new error message).

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#52 (retry/backoff for scheduled jobs):** both touch `internal/schedule`'s job semantics; this one is confined to add-time parsing and lands independently.
- **#55 (run observability):** a status surface would have made this failure *visible*; this fix makes it *impossible*. Both are worth having.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: Trailing --deliver with no value is swallowed into the cron prompt: job is silently created with delivery disabled and a corrupted prompt

## Motivation

`waffle ws close` is the **only destructive** workspace verb — it tears down the container and volume. Its guard rails (refusing on dirty/unpushed work unless `--force`) assume the command is operating on the workspace the user *meant*. The current argument parse breaks that assumption: it cannot tell "one id" from "several tokens, last one wins", so a fat-fingered extra token, a shell glob expansion, or a mistyped flag silently redirects the teardown to a workspace the user never named.

Every sibling command already gets this right — `close` is the one destructive handler without an arity check.

## Current behaviour

`cmd/waffle/ws_cmd.go:75-87`:

```go
case "close":
    force := false
    id := ""
    for _, a := range args[1:] {
        if a == "--force" {
            force = true
        } else {
            id = a
        }
    }
    if id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("usage: waffle ws close <id> [--force]")
    }
```

Three distinct failure classes fall out of "last non-`--force` token wins":

1. **Extra positional** — `waffle ws close abc123 def456` closes `def456`. The user named `abc123`; nothing warns them. The output even helpfully reports `def456`'s dirty files (`ws_cmd.go:91-93`), reinforcing the illusion the right workspace was processed.
2. **Mistyped flag** — `waffle ws close abc123 --froce` sets `id = "--froce"` (overwriting `abc123`) and attempts to close a workspace literally named `--froce`. Errors, but with a baffling message, and the typo'd `--force` intent is silently dropped.
3. **Shell glob** — an unquoted pattern that expands to multiple words closes whichever expansion sorted last.

Contrast with the siblings, all strict: `open` (`ws_cmd.go:46-48`), `idle` (`ws_cmd.go:64-66`), `cron rm` (`cmd/waffle/cron_cmd.go:62-64`) — each `if len(args) != 2 { return usage }`.

## Impact

Destructive operation on an unintended target, with misleading success/diagnostic output. The unpushed-work refusal limits (but does not eliminate) data loss: a clean-but-wanted workspace is torn down with no recovery, and with `--force` in the command line even the dirty guard is bypassed for the wrong target. Severity: low likelihood, high badness, trivial fix — classic arity bug.

## Proposed change

Parse strictly: exactly one positional id plus an optional `--force`, order-independent; everything else is a usage error.

```go
force := false
id := ""
for _, a := range args[1:] {
    switch {
    case a == "--force":
        force = true
    case strings.HasPrefix(a, "-"):
        return fmt.Errorf("unknown flag %q\nusage: waffle ws close <id> [--force]", a)
    case id != "":
        return fmt.Errorf("expected one workspace id, got %q and %q\nusage: waffle ws close <id> [--force]", id, a)
    default:
        id = a
    }
}
```

Factor the parse into a small function (or table-test the `wsCmd` dispatch directly) so it is testable without Docker or a store.

### Non-goals

- No general flag-parsing framework adoption; the codebase's hand-rolled per-command parsing is a deliberate style (`cron_cmd.go`, `chat_cmd.go` do the same). This issue only brings `close` up to the strictness of its siblings.
- Duplicate `--force` handling (idempotent today) does not need to become an error.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `waffle ws close <a> <b>` is rejected with a usage error that names **both** conflicting tokens, before any store lookup or Docker call is made.
- [ ] Any flag-shaped argument other than `--force` (leading `-`) is rejected with a usage error naming the unknown flag — it is never treated as a workspace id.
- [ ] `--force` is accepted in either position: `ws close <id> --force` and `ws close --force <id>` both work and both set force.
- [ ] `ws close` with no id still returns the usage error (existing behaviour preserved).
- [ ] On any parse rejection the process exits non-zero and no workspace mutation occurs — verified by test (no `Manager.Close`/`Idle` invocation; the parse must fail before the manager is constructed or via a stub).
- [ ] Unit tests (table-driven) cover at minimum: `close a b` → error naming `a` and `b`; `close a --froce` → error naming `--froce`; `close a --force` → ok/force; `close --force a` → ok/force; `close` → usage; `close --force` → usage.
- [ ] No behaviour change to `ls`/`open`/`idle`.

## Interactions with existing issues

- **#48 (ws CLI races a running serve):** same file and same command surface; whichever lands second rebases trivially. This fix is strictly local and does not depend on #48's coordination design.
- **#36 (workspace idle/TTL):** auto-close introduced there must go through `Manager.Close` with the unpushed-work guard, not through this CLI path — no interaction beyond shared semantics.

---

*Expanded to a full specification from the original audit finding; all file:line references verified against `main` @ cde1b22 (2026-07-08).*
title: ws close parses args positionally with no arity check: an extra or mistyped token silently selects a different workspace for destructive teardown
