## Problem
In the `/repo` handler, `c.current` is switched to the workspace session **unconditionally**, but `c.history`/`c.persisted` are refreshed only inside the `if turns, err := c.sessions.Turns(...); err == nil` success branch. On a transient `Turns` error, `c.current` points at the new session while `c.history`/`c.persisted` still hold the previous session's data.

## Where
- `cmd/waffle/chat_cmd.go:258-266` — `Turns` success branch updates history/persisted; `c.current = sess` runs regardless.

## Impact
After a transient read error: the next `turn()` (a) feeds the old, unrelated session's history to the model as context, and (b) persists the new user turn into the *new* session ID keyed off the *stale* `c.persisted` index, writing an orphaned turn. The session's stored history and the in-memory context permanently disagree; `waffle chat -c` later shows a single orphaned turn.

## Proposed solution
Only switch `c.current` after `Turns` succeeds — move `c.current = sess` inside the success branch, and on error surface it and leave the session unchanged (or fully reset history/persisted/current together atomically). Add a test where `Turns` errors and assert `c.current` is unchanged.
title: /repo desyncs in-memory history from the current session when loading turns fails

body:
## Problem
`Scheduler.Run` reads the job list from the store exactly once at startup, registers those jobs with cron, then blocks on `<-ctx.Done()`. There is no reload/watch, so jobs added or re-enabled while `serve` is running never fire until the whole process is restarted.

## Where
- `internal/schedule/schedule.go:198` — single `s.Store.List(ctx)`
- `internal/schedule/schedule.go:204-214` — register loop
- `internal/schedule/schedule.go:216-217` — `c.Start()` then block on `<-ctx.Done()` (no reload)
- created once at `cmd/waffle/serve_cmd.go:82`

## Impact
`waffle cron add ...` (or re-enabling a disabled job) during a live `serve` silently has no effect — the job never runs, with no error surfaced — a confusing "my scheduled job didn't run" bug.

## Proposed solution
Reconcile the cron set with the store periodically or on demand. Options: a ticker that re-lists jobs and diffs against the registered entries (add new, remove deleted, update changed cron specs); or have `cron add`/enable signal the running scheduler (e.g. via a channel or a lightweight notify) to reload. Track registered `cron.EntryID`s per job id so updates/removals are precise. Add a test that adds a job after `Run` has started and asserts it fires.
title: Scheduler never reloads jobs: cron add/enable during serve has no effect until restart

body:
## Problem
`Workspace.Open` resumes an existing workspace only when `ForRepo` returns `err == nil`. `ForRepo`/`scanOne` return *any* error (including transient `SQLITE_BUSY`) — not just `sql.ErrNoRows` — so a transient DB error is treated identically to "no existing workspace", and `Open` proceeds to create a fresh session/container/volume.

## Where
- `internal/workspace/workspace.go:139` — `if existing, err := m.ForRepo(ctx, repo); err == nil { ...resume... }`
- `internal/workspace/workspace.go:509-519` — `scanOne` maps `sql.ErrNoRows` to "workspace not found" but returns other errors verbatim (also non-nil)

## Impact
On a transient read error for a repo that already has a healthy workspace, `Open` spins up a new container + volume + session and mints a token, then hits the partial unique index on INSERT. Best case it churns real Docker resources and recovers via the race path; if `isUniqueConstraintError` doesn't match the driver string (see the sibling issue) it returns a hard failure for a repo that was actually fine.

## Proposed solution
Have `Open` branch on the error kind: only proceed to create when the lookup is a definitive not-found (a sentinel `ErrWorkspaceNotFound` from `scanOne` via `errors.Is`); on any other error, return it (or retry) rather than creating a duplicate. Add a test injecting a transient error from `ForRepo` and asserting no new container/volume is created.
title: Workspace Open treats a transient DB error as 'no workspace' and churns a duplicate container/volume

body:
## Problem
The dead-runner detection branches run only `if herr == nil`, but `lastHealth` uses a 500ms timeout and returns a non-nil error precisely under the `outbound.db` lock contention the detector is meant to survive. So when the runner is genuinely dead *and* the queue is contended, detection is skipped and `Exec` blocks until the caller ctx or the full 11-minute `DefaultToolTimeout`.

## Where
- `internal/sandbox/client.go:94` — `if herr == nil {` gates both dead-runner branches
- `internal/sandbox/client.go:115-126` — `lastHealth` uses `context.WithTimeout(ctx, 500*time.Millisecond)`; returns the error on deadline/contention
- `internal/sandbox/queue.go:69` — queue DB `busy_timeout(5000)` (5s) exceeds the 500ms health cap
- `internal/sandbox/docker.go:118` — `DefaultToolTimeout` (11 min) is the fallback bound

## Impact
The fast-fail design is defeated exactly when it matters: a dead runner under bind-mount lock contention leaves the caller blocked for up to 11 minutes instead of failing quickly.

## Proposed solution
Distinguish "health probe couldn't run" from "runner is alive". On `lastHealth` deadline/contention, don't silently treat it as healthy — e.g. track consecutive probe failures and, past a threshold within the no-heartbeat window, run `attemptShutdown` and fail fast; or raise the `lastHealth` timeout above the queue `busy_timeout` so a genuine result is obtained; or fall back to a container-liveness check (`docker inspect`) when the SQLite probe times out. Add a test with a contended/oversized busy window and a dead runner.
title: Dead-runner detection is disabled under queue lock contention (Exec blocks up to 11 minutes)

body:
## Problem
`runnerNoHealthWait` (10s) is measured from the start of `Exec`, not from runner readiness. `StartDocker` returns as soon as `docker run -d` creates the container; the in-container `waffle runner` may still be booting. A first tool call issued before the runner emits its first heartbeat can falsely declare a healthy runner dead.

## Where
- `internal/sandbox/client.go:72` — `start := time.Now()` (Exec entry)
- `internal/sandbox/client.go:92,100` — `waited := time.Since(start)` … `else if waited > runnerNoHealthWait { attemptShutdown(...); return "...no runner heartbeat seen" }`
- `internal/sandbox/docker.go:72-88` — `StartDocker` detached run, no readiness handshake
- `internal/sandbox/runner.go:50-59` — runner only begins heartbeating after its own init

## Impact
The first tool call on a freshly started sandbox whose image/runner takes >10s to reach the heartbeat loop (large image, slow disk, cold start) is aborted with "runner appears dead (no runner heartbeat seen)", and the runner is shut down — killing a perfectly healthy sandbox on first use.

## Proposed solution
Measure the no-heartbeat window from runner readiness, not Exec entry. Either (a) have `StartDocker` block until the first heartbeat row appears (bounded readiness handshake) before returning, or (b) record the container start time and only apply `runnerNoHealthWait` relative to it, or (c) treat "no heartbeat yet, container young" as "still starting" and keep polling up to a separate, longer startup budget. Add a test simulating a slow first heartbeat.
title: Cold sandbox container falsely declared dead on first tool call (>10s startup)

body:
## Problem
In the OpenAI streaming accumulator, assistant text and tool-call arguments are counted against a **single** shared byte budget (`maxBytes`). When the cap is hit, **all** accumulated tool calls are discarded and `StopToolUse` is rewritten to `StopEndTurn` — so a legitimate tool call can be silently dropped and the agent loop treats the turn as complete.

## Where
- `internal/llm/openaip/openai.go:240,247` — text increments `currentSize`
- `internal/llm/openaip/openai.go:273,279` — tool-call args increment the same `currentSize`
- `internal/llm/openaip/openai.go:300` — on cap: `toolCalls = map[int]*wireToolCall{}` (all dropped)
- `internal/llm/openaip/openai.go:301-303` — `StopToolUse` rewritten to `StopEndTurn`
- `internal/agent/agent.go:101` — `resp.StopReason != llm.StopToolUse` → `Run` returns as "done"

## Impact
A model that emits a lot of reasoning text followed by a valid, budget-respecting tool call can have its tool call thrown away; the requested tool never runs and the turn ends with a truncation-warning text block instead. Verified PLAUSIBLE: `maxBytes = min(MaxTokens*8, 2MiB)` while output is ~`MaxTokens*4` bytes typical, so it triggers with byte-heavy (multibyte/CJK) output or a deliberately low configured `MaxTokens`.

## Proposed solution
Do not let text spend budget that then starves tool calls. Options: track separate budgets for text vs tool-call arguments; or when the cap is hit, **preserve** already-complete tool calls and keep `StopToolUse` (truncate only the streamed text). Preserving the tool_use blocks keeps the loop functioning. Add a test where text nearly fills the budget and a subsequent tool call must still be returned.
title: Shared byte budget can silently drop a valid tool call and end the turn (OpenAI streaming)

body:
## Problem
The OpenAI-compatible provider requests streaming (`Stream: true`) but never sends `stream_options: {"include_usage": true}`. OpenAI's streaming API omits the `usage` object unless that option is set, so `resp.Usage` is always zero for the OpenAI provider.

## Where
- `internal/llm/openaip/openai.go:64-70` — `wireRequest` struct has no `stream_options` field
- `internal/llm/openaip/openai.go:139` — `toWire` sets `Stream: true` and nothing else
- `internal/llm/openaip/openai.go:223-226` — `chunk.Usage != nil` branch never fires against strict OpenAI

## Impact
Token accounting — the very thing `agent.go` describes as guarding "the credit card" — is silently always 0 for OpenAI/OpenRouter and any strict-OpenAI-compatible backend. Usage-based limits, logging, and cost tracking are wrong. (Some lenient compatible endpoints emit usage anyway; the bug is specific to spec-compliant ones.)

## Proposed solution
Add `StreamOptions *struct{ IncludeUsage bool }` (json `stream_options`) to `wireRequest` and set `include_usage: true` when `Stream` is true. Handle the final usage-only chunk (which has an empty `choices` array). Add a test asserting the request body includes `stream_options.include_usage` and that a usage-bearing final chunk populates `resp.Usage`.
title: OpenAI provider token usage is always zero (missing stream_options.include_usage)

body:
## Problem
`InitIdentity`'s overwrite guard only refuses when `LoadIdentity()` returns a **nil** error. `LoadIdentity` maps any non-`ErrNotFound` keyring failure to a wrapped non-nil error, so a *transient* keyring read failure (keychain locked, DBus/timeout) while an identity actually exists bypasses the guard and `keyring.Set` overwrites the existing identity — permanently destroying access to `secrets.age`.

## Where
- `internal/secret/identity.go:54-56` — `if _, err := LoadIdentity(); err == nil { return ... "refusing to overwrite" }`
- `internal/secret/identity.go:40-41` — `LoadIdentity` returns `fmt.Errorf("%w (keyring unavailable: %v)", ErrNoIdentity, err)` for any non-not-found error
- `internal/secret/identity.go:62` — `keyring.Set(...)` runs when the guard is skipped

## Impact
`waffle secret init` run while the keyring backend is momentarily unavailable generates a brand-new X25519 identity and overwrites the stored one. All existing secrets, encrypted to the old recipient, become permanently undecryptable. Silent, irreversible data loss. Severity: **high**.

## Failure scenario
An identity already exists; the OS keyring returns a transient read error on `Get` (locked keychain) while `Set` still succeeds → guard's `err == nil` is false → fall through to `keyring.Set` → old identity gone.

## Proposed solution
Refuse on anything other than a definitive not-found. Have the guard branch on the error *kind*:
- `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` (or `ErrNoIdentity`) → safe to create.
- `nil` → identity exists → refuse.
- any other error → **refuse** ("keyring unavailable; cannot verify existing identity — refusing to overwrite"), do not create.

Add a test injecting a transient keyring error and asserting no overwrite occurs.
title: waffle secret init can overwrite the identity on a transient keyring error (irreversible secret-store data loss)

body:
## Problem
`serve` starts the scheduler as a fire-and-forget goroutine and returns as soon as `gw.Run(ctx)` returns, without ever awaiting the scheduler. `defer cleanup()` then closes the **shared** sandbox executor and MCP clients while an in-flight cron job may still be driving them → use-after-close.

## Where
- `cmd/waffle/serve_cmd.go:46` — `defer cleanup()` (closes shared sandbox executor + MCP clients)
- `cmd/waffle/serve_cmd.go:92-96` — scheduler goroutine, never awaited
- `cmd/waffle/serve_cmd.go:99` — `return gw.Run(ctx)` (waits for gateway handlers only)
- `internal/schedule/schedule.go:217-219` — the scheduler's own in-flight-job wait (`c.Stop()`) lives *inside* the un-awaited goroutine, so it is invisible to `serveCmd`.

## Impact
On SIGTERM with the gateway idle, `gw.Run` returns near-instantly, `serveCmd` returns, and `cleanup()` closes the SQLite queue handles / `docker rm -f`s the container while a cron job's `Runner.Run → Agent.Run → sandbox Exec` is still polling `outbound.db`. Result: `sql: database is closed` / missing-container errors, and `markRun` records a spurious failure during what should be a clean drain.

## Proposed solution
Await the scheduler before running cleanup. E.g. run the scheduler with its own `sync.WaitGroup`/errgroup and `wg.Wait()` (or block on the scheduler goroutine) after `gw.Run` returns and before `cleanup()` executes. Ensure `Scheduler.Run`'s in-flight-job drain (`c.Stop()`) completes before shared resources are torn down. Add a test that SIGTERMs mid-cron-job and asserts no use-after-close.
title: serve shutdown closes shared sandbox/MCP while a cron job is still running (use-after-close)

body:
## Problem
On graceful shutdown the gateway drains in-flight handlers using the **same context that was just canceled**, so the in-flight turn is aborted mid-execution and also fails to persist — the opposite of the documented "drain rather than abandon" intent.

## Where
- `internal/gateway/gateway.go:70-71` — comment: "shutdown drains work already accepted rather than abandoning it mid-turn"
- `internal/gateway/gateway.go:99` — `g.handle(ctx, msg)` launched with the loop `ctx`
- `internal/gateway/gateway.go:202` — `g.Agent.Run(ctx, ...)` and `:209` — `g.Sessions.AppendTurn(ctx, ...)` both receive the canceled ctx. `AppendTurn` → `BeginTx(ctx)`/`ExecContext(ctx)` return `context.Canceled` immediately.

## Impact
When SIGINT/SIGTERM arrives while a turn is running: `Agent.Run` returns `context.Canceled`, `converse` returns an error, and any `AppendTurn` fails — so the user's message and the partial assistant turn are neither completed nor saved. `handlers.Wait()` returns quickly because the goroutines abort rather than finish.

## Proposed solution
Derive a detached drain context for accepted work, e.g. `drainCtx := context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (optionally with a bounded `context.WithTimeout`), and pass it into `handle`/`Agent.Run`/`AppendTurn` for the in-flight turn on the shutdown path — while still using the cancelable `ctx` to stop *accepting* new messages. Add a test that cancels mid-turn and asserts the turn is persisted.
title: Graceful shutdown abandons and fails to persist the in-flight turn (canceled ctx in drain path)

body:
## Problem
`agent.prepareContext` injects a context-summary message with `Role: RoleAssistant` as the **first** message sent to the provider, on every conversation longer than `recentWindow` (20 messages). The Anthropic Messages API rejects a request whose first message is not `user` role (and rejects consecutive same-role messages), so the request fails with a 400.

## Where
- `internal/agent/agent.go:208` — `Role: llm.RoleAssistant,`
- `internal/agent/agent.go:221` — `return append([]llm.Message{sumMsg}, recent...)` (summary is element 0)
- `internal/llm/anthropicp/anthropic.go:101-114` — `toParams` maps the role straight through; it does not prepend/coalesce/reorder, so nothing repairs the leading-assistant message.

## Impact
Any Anthropic-backed session that exceeds 20 messages triggers the summarize path and then fails at the provider with `messages: first message must use the "user" role` / `roles must alternate`. Long-running conversations break. If the recent window also begins on an assistant turn, two consecutive assistant messages are produced as well.

## Failure scenario
Chat on the Anthropic provider until history > 20 messages → next turn calls `prepareContext` → request `messages[0]` has role `assistant` → HTTP 400, turn errors out.

## Proposed solution
Make the injected summary a `RoleUser` message (the labeling text already defends against prompt injection), **or** carry it as extra `System` text on the `Request` instead of as a message. If kept as a message, also guarantee alternation at the window boundary (e.g. ensure the first `recent` message is a user turn, or merge the summary into the first user message). Add a provider-translation test asserting the first outgoing Anthropic message is always `user` role.
title: Long conversations 400 on Anthropic: context summary injected as leading assistant message
